overview: Palantir builds software platforms -- Gotham, Foundry, Apollo, and the Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) -- that integrate organizations' data, decisions, and operations, acting as a central operating system for customers. It was founded in 2003 serving the U.S. intelligence and defense community (Gotham) and later expanded into commercial enterprises (Foundry), with AIP (launched 2023) now the primary growth engine connecting large language models to customer data and workflows under governance and security constraints. The company operates two reportable segments, government and commercial, generating 51% and 49% of nine-month 2026 revenue respectively, with 81% of revenue from U.S. customers.

business_model.summary: Palantir sells multi-year subscriptions to its hosted software (Palantir Cloud), term software licenses deployed in customer environments (On-Premises Software), and professional services, all recognized ratably over the contract term. Growth is driven by expanding usage within existing accounts (average revenue per top-20 customer grew 76% YoY to $146M in the TTM ended Q3 2026) and by AIP-led 'bootcamps'/pilots that convert into large enterprise and government deployments. Gross margins are high (85% for the nine months ended September 2026) and the business generated $3.3 billion of operating cash flow over the same period with no outstanding debt.
business_model.customer_type: Large enterprise (B2B) and government/defense/intelligence agencies; 1,090 customers as of Q3 2026 (up from 911 a year earlier)
business_model.geographic_mix: United States 81% of nine-month 2026 revenue (growing share), Rest of World 19% (no single non-U.S. country individually material)

main_competitors: Traditional government IT integrators (Leidos, Booz Allen, SAIC)
competitive_position.market_position: Incumbent leader in government/defense data integration (two decades of security accreditations) and an emerging leader in enterprise AI operationalization via AIP; no single competitor matches the full Gotham/Foundry/Apollo/AIP stack, though point solutions compete on individual layers

moat_factors.description: Decades of security clearances, FedRAMP/IL5-6 accreditations, and classified deployment experience that would take new entrants 5-10 years to replicate
Once an organization's data, logic, and workflows are mapped into Palantir's Ontology layer, migrating off becomes costly and operationally disruptive
Embedding engineers directly with customers accelerates adoption and deepens relationships, but is labor-intensive and resembles a consulting model more than pure SaaS
$10.4B in cash and Treasuries with no outstanding debt gives flexibility to invest in compute capacity and sales capacity ahead of competitors

weaknesses: Forward-deployed engineering/pilot ('bootcamp') model is more services-intensive than typical SaaS, raising questions about scalability of margins as the customer base grows
Hyperscalers (Microsoft Fabric, AWS, Google) are bundling comparable data/AI orchestration into existing cloud contracts, a channel advantage Palantir lacks
Heavy reliance on continued U.S. government and defense spending growth, which is politically and budget-cycle dependent
High stock-based compensation and insider selling create ongoing dilution and sentiment overhang

growth_drivers: AIP adoption driving a step-change in U.S. commercial growth (148% YoY revenue growth in Q3 2026)
Expansion within existing large government and commercial accounts (top-20 customer average revenue up 76% YoY)
U.S. Army 10-year, ~$10 billion enterprise data-modernization agreement consolidating prior contracts

New and renewed international government deals, including a renewed ~£240 million UK Ministry of Defence contract and a DHS business purchase agreement allowing up to $1 billion of agency purchases without competitive bidding
Rising allied-nation defense and intelligence AI spending amid heightened geopolitical tensions
Large committed cloud/compute capacity ($5.6 billion minimum spend over 10 years, amended March 2026) to support AI workload growth
Remaining performance obligations of $4.9 billion as of Q3 2026, providing visibility into forward revenue

business.description: Government revenue (51% of total) is subject to federal/allied budget cycles, continuing resolutions, shutdowns, and administration priorities that can delay or reduce contract awards
Explosive U.S. commercial growth may partly reflect enterprises 'catching up' on AI adoption; a slowdown in AIP pilot conversions would pressure the growth narrative embedded in the valuation

business.risk: Competition from hyperscalers and in-house build
business.description: Microsoft, Google, and AWS are embedding competing AI/data-orchestration tools directly into cloud contracts customers already hold; large enterprises are also building in-house data/AI teams

business.risk: No single customer >10% of revenue, but concentration in top accounts
business.description: One customer represented 25-27% of accounts receivable in recent periods, and the top 20 customers are an outsized share of revenue growth

financial.description: SBC was $786 million for the nine months ended September 2026 (~13% of revenue), creating ongoing dilution even as GAAP profitability has turned solidly positive
Shares have traded at triple-digit trailing P/E multiples; any growth deceleration or AI-sentiment reversal could trigger outsized multiple compression

regulatory.description: Reporting on a 2026 Deputy Secretary of Defense memo and other awards highlighted contracts and funding pledges that bypassed standard FAR competitive-bidding/justification processes, inviting political and oversight scrutiny

regulatory.risk: Data privacy, surveillance, and human-rights criticism
regulatory.description: Palantir's work with U.S. immigration enforcement and other security agencies has drawn civil-liberties criticism and reputational/political risk that could affect future public-sector relationships
Evolving AI governance rules in the U.S., U.K., and EU could add compliance costs or constrain certain use cases of AIP

macro.description: Palantir's growth is linked to the broader enterprise AI investment cycle; a pullback in AI capex sentiment (as voiced by bears such as Michael Burry) could compress sentiment-driven valuation regardless of fundamentals
Ongoing conflicts (Russia-Ukraine, Middle East) have not been described by the company as material to results, but increase both demand for defense software and tail-risk disruption
As a high-multiple growth name, PLTR's valuation is more sensitive to shifts in risk-free rates and risk appetite than cash-flow-mature peers

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Enterprise AI software and government/defense data-analytics spending are both in secular growth phases; defense budgets in the U.S. and allied nations are rising amid geopolitical tensions, and enterprises are accelerating AI adoption budgets
macro_factors.cyclicality: Government segment is relatively acyclical but budget-cycle dependent; commercial segment has more macro sensitivity but has so far shown resilience and acceleration through 2025-2026
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high indirect sensitivity via growth-stock valuation multiples; direct balance-sheet exposure is low given no debt and large cash/Treasury holdings generating interest income
key_input_costs: Third-party cloud hosting/compute (large multi-year commitments, e.g., $5.6B over 10 years)
Engineering and sales personnel (stock-based compensation heavy)

recent_developments.event: Q3 2026 results: revenue of $2.313B (+96% YoY), U.S. commercial revenue +148% YoY; raised FY2026 revenue guidance to $8.530-8.534B and adjusted free cash flow guidance to $4.8-5.0B; multiple sell-side analysts (Citi, Piper Sandler, Morgan Stanley, Barclays) raised price targets, while some bears (RBC, Freedom Capital Markets, Citron) maintained negative/cautious ratings despite raising targets

Reported media coverage of a Deputy Secretary of Defense memo pledging up to $243.9 million in additional Palantir software funding through March 2027, criticized for bypassing standard FAR sole-source justification procedures
Q2 2026 results showed U.S. government revenue growth of 90% YoY to $809 million, continuing the acceleration trend
Amended a major third-party cloud hosting agreement, committing to at least $5.6 billion of spend (with annual minimums of $268M-$979M) over 10 years through February 2036 to support AI compute needs
Heightened insider selling by CEO Alex Karp and founder Peter Thiel reported since February 2026, though much appears to be mechanical 10b5-1 plan activity tied to equity compensation

Renewed and expanded government relationships, including a ~£240 million, three-year UK Ministry of Defence contract (awarded without open competition under a defense exemption) and a DHS business purchase agreement enabling up to $1 billion of agency purchases without competitive bidding

items.notes: Implies ~91% YoY growth; raised from prior guidance following a 96% YoY revenue beat in Q3
Above consensus estimate of roughly $2.46 billion at the time of the print
Implies adjusted operating margin of roughly 62%, consistent with Q3 2026's 62% adjusted operating margin
Raised alongside the revenue guidance increase
Guidance raised from prior outlook after 148% YoY growth reported in Q3 2026

guidance.management_commentary: Management highlighted accelerating revenue growth across both segments, record contribution margins (70% government, 77% commercial in Q3 2026), and continued expansion of remaining performance obligations ($4.9 billion), framing AIP adoption as still in early stages across both government and commercial customer bases.

bull_case: Durable, accelerating growth: revenue growth has accelerated from the 20s% to the 90s% YoY over the past two years, with both government (+81% YoY in Q3 2026) and commercial (+113% YoY) segments contributing

High and improving profitability: 85% gross margin, ~62% adjusted operating margin, and $3.3 billion of operating cash flow over nine months of 2026, funded without any debt and with $10.4 billion of cash/Treasuries
Deep moat in government/defense from two decades of security accreditations and incumbency, reinforced by large multi-year agreements (e.g., the ~$10 billion U.S. Army enterprise deal)

AIP positions Palantir as potential foundational 'enterprise AI operating layer,' with bootcamp-to-contract conversion driving outsized commercial expansion and rising average revenue per top customer
Secular tailwinds from rising global defense/intelligence budgets and accelerating enterprise AI adoption benefit both of Palantir's segments simultaneously
bear_case: Valuation is priced for continued hypergrowth (trailing/forward P/E multiples well above software peers); any deceleration or AI-sentiment reversal could trigger sharp multiple compression, as flagged by bears including Michael Burry and Citron Research

Government revenue concentration and dependence on favorable budget/political conditions, with recent no-bid/sole-source contract awards drawing oversight scrutiny that could constrain future deal structures

Commercial growth may partly reflect a one-time 'catch-up' pull-forward in enterprise AI adoption rather than a fully durable run-rate, especially if hyperscalers bundle comparable AI/data tools into existing cloud contracts at lower incremental cost

Forward-deployed engineering model is more services-intensive than a typical SaaS business, raising questions about long-run margin scalability as the customer base broadens beyond the largest accounts
Heavy, sustained insider selling by the CEO and founders, combined with meaningful stock-based compensation dilution, create an ongoing sentiment and share-count overhang
